title: Ezra 1:1–11
context: The book opens in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia. The LORD stirs up Cyrus’s spirit so that he issues a written decree: the LORD, the God of heaven, has given him the kingdoms of the earth and has commanded him to build a house in Jerusalem. Exiles may go up and build, and neighbors are to help them with silver, gold, goods, animals, and a free will offering. The heads of Judah and Benjamin, with priests and Levites, rise up, “all whose spirit God had stirred to go up,” and Cyrus releases the temple vessels once taken by Nebuchadnezzar, counted out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah. The unit is shared ground about God’s faithfulness: “the LORD’s word by Jeremiah’s mouth might be accomplished,” the promise of return after the years of exile named in Jeremiah 25:11–12 and 29:10. The same decree closes 2 Chronicles 36:22–23, already drafted in this worktree, in nearly the same words, though Chronicles cuts the invitation shorter and this chapter continues with helpers, vessels, and Sheshbazzar. Readers often also connect Cyrus with Isaiah 44:28–45:1, where he is named in connection with Jerusalem and the temple’s foundation; this chapter itself does not quote those lines, and the link should be held as a related text, not as a claim this narrative makes in so many words. Nothing beyond the text is added in explaining Cyrus’s own motives: what is given is the LORD stirring him, and the decree spoken in his name. Sheshbazzar’s relation to Zerubbabel, who will head the list in 2:2, is left as an open question, with more than one serious option. Both traditions read the chapter as the LORD keeping his word and opening the way home, without a party contrast over the decree or the vessels.

verses.text: Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the LORD’s word by Jeremiah’s mouth might be accomplished, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and put it also in writing, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the LORD’s word by Jeremiah’s mouth might be accomplished, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia,” so that he made a proclamation in writing. The usual references for that word are Jeremiah 25:11–12 and 29:10, the seventy years and the promise of return. How those years are counted is discussed, as the already drafted 2 Chronicles 36:21–22 notes also say. The two openings are nearly the same. This verse is shared ground about God’s faithfulness, not a puzzle about the emperor’s private reasons.

Arminian readers hear a real act of God in history: he stirs a foreign king so that Jeremiah’s word comes to pass, and Cyrus truly issues the decree.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from the LORD’s initiative. The LORD stirs up the spirit of a king, and the word spoken by Jeremiah is accomplished, the same emphasis already made at the close of 2 Chronicles 36.

Both traditions take the verse as God’s faithfulness to his word, and they refuse to invent motives for Cyrus beyond what is written here.

verses.text: “Cyrus king of Persia says, ‘The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth; and he has commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Cyrus says, “The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth; and he has commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah.” The decree names the LORD as the God of heaven and claims a commission to build his house. 2 Chronicles 36:23 has the same opening words. The notes stay with what the proclamation says and do not settle whether Cyrus spoke from deep knowledge of Israel’s God or from some other policy.

Arminian readers take the written claim seriously as the means God uses, a real command to build, without reading a full conversion story into the sentence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear the LORD as the one who gives kingdoms and commands the house to be built. The king’s words serve that purpose; his inner life is not described.

Both traditions keep the verse as the public ground of the return and the temple work, consistent with the drafted Chronicles notes, and invent no contrast over Cyrus’s heart.

verses.text: Whoever there is among you of all his people, may his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel (he is God), which is in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Whoever there is among you of all his people, may his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel (he is God), which is in Jerusalem.” The invitation is wider than the shorter close of 2 Chronicles 36:23, which ends at “let him go up.” Here the goers are to build the house, and the decree adds that the LORD, the God of Israel, is God.

Arminian readers hear a genuine opening for any of the people to go up, with God being with him, and a clear charge to rebuild the house.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also stress the confession in the decree itself: the LORD, the God of Israel, is God, and the house in Jerusalem is his. The longer form of the invitation belongs to this book and should not be trimmed to the Chronicles ending.

Both traditions read a real permission to return and build, without forcing the two closings into one wording.

verses.text: Whoever is left, in any place where he lives, let the men of his place help him with silver, with gold, with goods, and with animals, in addition to the free will offering for God’s house which is in Jerusalem.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Those who remain in any place are to help the one who goes “with silver, with gold, with goods, and with animals, in addition to the free will offering for God’s house which is in Jerusalem.” The return is not only a march of volunteers; neighbors are charged to support them, and a free will offering for the house is named beside that help.

Arminian readers take the help and the offering as real gifts, freely given in addition to the travel support, not as a tax in all but name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see provision for the house arising under the decree. Silver, gold, goods, and animals, plus the free will offering, are the means by which the work can begin.

Both traditions keep the verse as practical support for the return and the temple, without a contrast over the offering.

verses.text: Then the heads of fathers’ households of Judah and Benjamin, the priests and the Levites, all whose spirit God had stirred to go up, rose up to build the LORD’s house which is in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
The heads of fathers’ households of Judah and Benjamin, the priests, and the Levites rise up, “all whose spirit God had stirred to go up,” to build the LORD’s house in Jerusalem. The same verb of stirring used of Cyrus in 1:1 is now used of the people who actually go. Judah and Benjamin, with the temple ministers, are named as the core of this first return.

Arminian readers hear a real response: God stirs their spirit, and they rise up to go, a willing act that the verse itself describes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hold both sides of the line. God stirs the goers, as he stirred the king, and the heads, priests, and Levites do rise up to build.

Both traditions take the stirring of king and people as shared ground, God’s faithfulness producing a real departure for Jerusalem.

verses.text: All those who were around them strengthened their hands with vessels of silver, with gold, with goods, with animals, and with precious things, in addition to all that was willingly offered.
verses.arminianNotes:
Those around them “strengthened their hands with vessels of silver, with gold, with goods, with animals, and with precious things, in addition to all that was willingly offered.” The support promised in the decree is now given, and willing offerings are again named in addition.

Arminian readers hear neighbors actually strengthening the goers’ hands, a historical fulfillment of 1:4, including gifts willingly offered.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read the verse as the decree at work: silver, gold, goods, animals, and precious things are placed in their hands, besides the willing gifts.

Both traditions keep the line as a report of help for the journey and the house, not as a type to be pressed.

verses.text: Also Cyrus the king brought out the vessels of the LORD’s house, which Nebuchadnezzar had brought out of Jerusalem, and had put in the house of his gods;
verses.arminianNotes:
Cyrus also “brought out the vessels of the LORD’s house, which Nebuchadnezzar had brought out of Jerusalem, and had put in the house of his gods”. The vessels taken at the exile, already told in 2 Kings 24–25 and 2 Chronicles 36, are now brought out of that pagan house to be returned. The king’s role here is to restore what had been seized.

Arminian readers take the restoration as a real reversal of the earlier plunder, the LORD’s house remembered in the return of its vessels.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see the same reversal under God’s hand. What Nebuchadnezzar placed in the house of his gods is brought out by Cyrus for Jerusalem.

Both traditions read the verse as the recovery of the holy vessels, without a contrast over the king’s part in it.

verses.text: even those, Cyrus king of Persia brought out by the hand of Mithredath the treasurer, and counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
The vessels are brought out “by the hand of Mithredath the treasurer, and counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah.” Mithredath is named as a Persian treasurer; no further biography is invented for him. Sheshbazzar, called the prince of Judah, receives the count. Sheshbazzar’s identity is not settled here. Some readers take him to be the same man as Zerubbabel, who heads the list in 2:2; some keep him as a distinct official who leads this first handing over; some compare the name with Shenazzar in 1 Chronicles 3:18. Later, Ezra 5:14–16 will attribute the laying of the foundation to Sheshbazzar, while chapter 3 will describe the work under Zerubbabel and Jeshua. The options should be left open.

Arminian readers take Sheshbazzar as a real prince of Judah who receives the vessels, without choosing one identification as if the verse had made it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hedge the question. Sheshbazzar is the prince of Judah in this line, the vessels are counted out to him, and the relation to Zerubbabel remains discussed rather than decided.

Both traditions refuse to force a single identity and invent no party contrast over the name.

verses.text: This is the number of them: thirty platters of gold, one thousand platters of silver, twenty-nine knives,
verses.arminianNotes:
The count begins: “thirty platters of gold, one thousand platters of silver, twenty-nine knives,” The list is an inventory of returned vessels, item by item. The numbers should be read as a report of what was counted out, not as symbols, and not yet totaled.

Arminian readers take the gold and silver platters and the knives as real objects from the house, now on their way back.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the verse in the register of an inventory. Thirty, one thousand, and twenty-nine are the figures given here, and they will stand beside the further counts and the total in 1:11.

Both traditions refuse to allegorize the vessels or the numbers.

verses.text: thirty bowls of gold, four hundred ten silver bowls of a second kind, and one thousand other vessels.
verses.arminianNotes:
The inventory continues: “thirty bowls of gold, four hundred ten silver bowls of a second kind, and one thousand other vessels.” A second kind of silver bowl is distinguished, and a large group of other vessels is named without further sort. The notes leave that classification as the text gives it.

Arminian readers hear a careful count continuing, bowls of gold and of silver and a thousand other pieces, still as a list of objects.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the second kind and the other vessels as inventory language, not as a puzzle requiring a reconstruction the verse does not supply.

Both traditions wait for the total in the next verse and do not force a meaning onto the kinds.

verses.text: All the vessels of gold and of silver were five thousand four hundred. Sheshbazzar brought all these up when the captives were brought up from Babylon to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“All the vessels of gold and of silver were five thousand four hundred.” Sheshbazzar brings them up when the captives go up from Babylon to Jerusalem. The items numbered in 1:9–10, taken as they stand, do not add up to five thousand four hundred. The difference should be named and left unresolved; readers have suggested that the earlier lines list only some kinds, or that the totals are counted in different ways, but this verse does not explain the gap. Sheshbazzar remains the one who brings the vessels up, the same open identity already noted at 1:8.

Arminian readers take the journey of the captives and the vessels as a real return, and they refuse to hide the numerical tension or to invent a harmony.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also report both the listed figures and the total of five thousand four hundred, without declaring a solution. Sheshbazzar’s role as the one who brings them up is the narrative close of the chapter.

Both traditions leave the counts unharmonized and invent no doctrinal contrast from them.
